name: isalpha
prose: Returns a nonzero value (1) when c is an ASCII letter and 0 otherwise: islower(c) || isupper(c), that is (unsigned int)(c - 'a') < 26 or (unsigned int)(c - 'A') < 26. The subtractions c - 'a' and c - 'A' are signed int operations, so for c below INT_MIN + 97 (INT_MIN + 65 for the upper-case test) the signed subtraction overflows, which is undefined behaviour and can trap in checked builds; the function does not guard against that. It has no side effects.
note: nolibc/ctype.h:84-88. Reviewer (random testing: traps on an input meeting the precondition) right: signed overflow in c - 'a' for very negative c. Contract left empty.

name: isalnum
prose: Returns a nonzero value when c is an ASCII letter or digit and 0 otherwise: isalpha(c) || isdigit(c), where the digit test is (unsigned int)(c - '0') < 10 and isalpha tests the two letter ranges. The int subtractions c - 'a', c - 'A' and c - '0' overflow (undefined behaviour) for very negative c (below about INT_MIN + 97); the function does not guard against that. No side effects.
note: nolibc/ctype.h:90-94. Reviewer (random testing: traps on an input meeting the precondition) right for the same reason as isalpha. Contract left empty.

name: ispunct
prose: Returns a nonzero value when c is a printable non-space ASCII character that is not a letter or digit, and 0 otherwise: isgraph(c) && !isalnum(c), where isgraph tests (unsigned int)(c - 0x21) < 0x5e (characters 0x21 to 0x7e). The signed subtractions inside isgraph and isalnum overflow (undefined behaviour) for very negative c, which the function does not guard against; for c in the isgraph range the result excludes letters and digits. No side effects.
note: nolibc/ctype.h:96-100. Written from the code; the reviewer entry for this function was not shown in the compact listing, assumed to be the same random-testing trap comment. Contract left empty.

name: sys_lseek
prose: Raw system-call wrapper (nolibc, does not touch errno): fd, offset and whence are the lseek arguments. If __NR_lseek is defined it returns my_syscall3(__NR_lseek, fd, offset, whence) unchanged: the new file offset or a negative errno. Otherwise (32-bit targets with only llseek) it calls my_syscall5(__NR_llseek, fd, 0, offset, &loff, whence) with a 64-bit local loff initialised to 0; a negative result is returned as that negative errno; if the call succeeds but the 64-bit loff does not fit in off_t (loff != (off_t)loff) it returns -EOVERFLOW; otherwise it returns loff. The high word of the offset is passed as 0, so a negative offset is not sign-extended on this path.
note: nolibc/sys.h:591-612. Reviewer mechanical (contract omits EOVERFLOW): right; contract left empty because it depends on a system call.

name: waitpid
prose: Precondition: pid, status (may be NULL) and options as for waitpid(2). Returns the pid of the child whose state changed, or -1. If pid is INT_MIN it sets errno to ESRCH and returns -1. Otherwise it maps pid to a waitid selector: pid < -1 gives P_PGID with id -pid, pid == -1 gives P_ALL, pid == 0 gives P_PGID with id 0, pid > 0 gives P_PID with id pid; it ORs WEXITED into options and calls waitid(idtype, id, &info, options); a nonzero result returns -1 (errno is whatever waitid set). On success it converts info.si_code to a wait status written to *status when status is non-NULL: 0 gives 0; CLD_EXITED gives (si_status & 0xff) << 8; CLD_KILLED gives si_status & 0x7f; CLD_DUMPED gives (si_status & 0x7f) | 0x80; CLD_STOPPED and CLD_TRAPPED give (si_status << 8) + 0x7f; CLD_CONTINUED gives 0xffff. For any other si_code it returns -1 without setting errno and without writing *status. Otherwise it returns info.si_pid.
note: nolibc/sys/wait.h:37-97. Reviewer right: the default case (92-93) returns -1 with no SET_ERRNO call.

name: FS(lower_name, fs_name, upper_name)
prose: Template macro (tools/lib/api/fs/fs.c:107-145) instantiated for sysfs, procfs, debugfs, tracefs, hugetlbfs and bpf_fs (lines 147-152). Each instantiation defines a static struct fs fs__<lower_name> (name, known mount point list, magic number, initialised mutex) and these functions: lower_name_init_once(), which calls fs__init_once on that struct; <lower_name>__mountpoint(), which runs pthread_once with the init function and returns fs__mountpoint(fs), i.e. the cached fs->path (NULL if the file system was not found); <lower_name>__mount(), which returns the cached mount point if <lower_name>__mountpoint() is non-NULL and otherwise returns fs__mount(fs); and <lower_name>__configured(), which returns true exactly when <lower_name>__mountpoint() is non-NULL. fs__mount takes fs->mount_mutex, re-checks the cached path, otherwise calls mount_overload(fs) for a path, and if mount() succeeds and the mount validates against the magic number it stores a strdup of the path in fs->path; it returns the chosen mount point string even when the mount or validation failed (fs->path is then left NULL), and it unlocks the mutex on its single exit.
note: The listed item was the FS-macro generated trio; named by the macro head. Written from fs.c:107-145 and 253-291. mount_overload and fs__init_once not read.

name: sys_bpf_prog_load
prose: Precondition: attr points to a bpf_attr for BPF_PROG_LOAD of the given size; attempts is the maximum number of tries. It calls sys_bpf_fd(BPF_PROG_LOAD, attr, size), repeating while the result is negative, errno equals EAGAIN and --attempts is still greater than 0 (so attempts of 0 or 1 gives one call, and attempts n gives up to n calls), and returns the last fd. sys_bpf_fd uses the libc syscall() wrapper, so on failure the value returned is -1 with errno set (not a negative errno value), and on success it is a file descriptor that ensure_good_fd has moved above 2 if needed.
note: libbpf bpf.c:89-98; sys_bpf_fd (80-87), sys_bpf (74-78) and ensure_good_fd (libbpf_internal.h:656) read. Reviewer right: failure is -1 with errno set, not -errno. Contract left empty.

name: #define ___bpf_swab16(x) ((__u16)(
prose: Function-like macro, not a C function (tools/lib/bpf/bpf_endian.h:15-17): ___bpf_swab16(x) swaps the two bytes of x. It ORs ___bpf_mvb(x,16,0,1) and ___bpf_mvb(x,16,1,0), where ___bpf_mvb(x,b,n,m) takes byte n of x (byte 0 being the least significant), as a __u<b> value, and places it at byte position m; the result is cast to __u16. It evaluates x twice, so x should be a side-effect-free expression (it is used for compile-time constants).
note: bpf_endian.h:13-17. Previously dropped as a non-function; the macro does real arithmetic, kept as a fix with the macro head as its name.

name: #define ___bpf_swab32(x) ((__u32)(
prose: Function-like macro, not a C function (bpf_endian.h:19-23): ___bpf_swab32(x) reverses the four bytes of x by ORing ___bpf_mvb(x,32,n,3-n) for n = 0 to 3 (byte n of x, counted from the least significant, moved to byte position 3-n), cast to __u32. It evaluates x four times, so x should be a side-effect-free expression (it is used for compile-time constants).
note: bpf_endian.h:19-23. Previously dropped as a non-function; the macro does real arithmetic, kept as a fix with the macro head as its name.

name: #define ___bpf_swab64(x) ((__u64)(
prose: Function-like macro, not a C function (bpf_endian.h:25-33): ___bpf_swab64(x) reverses the eight bytes of x by ORing ___bpf_mvb(x,64,n,7-n) for n = 0 to 7, cast to __u64. It evaluates x eight times, so x should be a side-effect-free expression (it is used for compile-time constants).
note: bpf_endian.h:25-33. Previously dropped as a non-function; the macro does real arithmetic, kept as a fix with the macro head as its name.

name: #define bpf_htons(x)
prose: Function-like macro, not a C function (bpf_endian.h:80-82): chooses by __builtin_constant_p(x) between __bpf_constant_htons(x) and __bpf_htons(x). On a little-endian target the constant case is ___bpf_swab16(x) and the other case is __builtin_bswap16(x), so the 16-bit value is byte-swapped; on a big-endian target both cases are x unchanged. Any other byte order is a compile error (#error). It is the same for bpf_ntohs below.
note: bpf_endian.h:50-82. Previously dropped as a non-function; the macro does real arithmetic, kept as a fix with the macro head as its name.

name: #define bpf_ntohs(x)

On a little-endian target the constant case is ___bpf_swab16(x) and the other case is __builtin_bswap16(x), so the 16-bit network-order value is byte-swapped to host order; on a big-endian target both cases are x unchanged.

name: btf_dump_order_type
prose: Precondition: d is a btf_dump, id a type id, through_ptr says whether the path to this type went through a pointer. Returns 1 for a 'strong' definition, 0 for a type that needs no strong ordering, or a negative error. If the type's order_state is already ORDERED it returns 1. If it is ORDERING it returns 0 when the type is a named composite reached through a pointer (resolvable with a forward declaration), else logs and returns -ELOOP. Otherwise by BTF kind: INT and FLOAT set ORDERED and return 0. PTR calls itself on the target with through_ptr true, then sets ORDERED and returns that call's result (even if negative). ARRAY returns btf_dump_order_type on the element type with through_ptr false, and ARRAY, the modifiers (VOLATILE, CONST, RESTRICT, TYPE_TAG; which return the call on the target with the same through_ptr) and FUNC_PROTO (which orders the return type and every parameter type with the same through_ptr and returns 1 if any is strong, 0 if none, or the first negative error) never assign order_state in this function, so their state is left unchanged. STRUCT and UNION return 0 at once if through_ptr and named; otherwise they set ORDERING, order every member type (a negative result is returned immediately, leaving state ORDERING), add the type to the emit queue if it is named (btf_dump_add_emit_queue_id, error returned), set ORDERED and return 1. ENUM, ENUM64 and FWD add to the emit queue when named or not referenced (error returned), set ORDERED and return 1. TYPEDEF orders its target with the same through_ptr (a negative result returned), returns 0 if through_ptr and the target was not strong, otherwise adds the typedef to the emit queue (error returned), sets ORDERED and returns 1. FUNC, VAR, DATASEC and DECL_TAG set ORDERED and return 0. Any other kind returns -EINVAL.
note: slice cut the head; real function btf_dump.c:473-618. Reviewer WRONG: ARRAY, the modifier kinds and FUNC_PROTO do not set ORDERING at entry or anywhere (the comment at 482-483 says non-defining kinds never get an ordering state); only the defining kinds assign order_state.

name: btf_field_iter_init
prose: Precondition: it is the iterator to initialise, t a BTF type, iter_kind selects which fields to iterate (BTF_FIELD_ITER_IDS for type ids or BTF_FIELD_ITER_STRS for string offsets). It first resets the iterator (p = NULL, m_idx = -1, off_idx = 0, vlen = 0), then fills it->desc from the type's kind. For ITER_IDS: UNKN, INT, FLOAT, ENUM and ENUM64 have an empty descriptor; FWD, CONST, VOLATILE, RESTRICT, PTR, TYPEDEF, FUNC, VAR, DECL_TAG and TYPE_TAG have one field (the type member of btf_type); ARRAY has the element type and index type fields; STRUCT and UNION iterate the type field of each btf_member; FUNC_PROTO has the return type plus the type of each btf_param; DATASEC iterates the type of each btf_var_secinfo; any other kind returns -EINVAL. For ITER_STRS: UNKN is empty; INT, FLOAT, FWD, ARRAY, the modifiers, PTR, TYPEDEF, FUNC, VAR, DECL_TAG, TYPE_TAG and DATASEC have the type's name_off; ENUM, ENUM64, STRUCT/UNION and FUNC_PROTO have name_off plus the name_off of each enumerator, member or parameter; any other kind returns -EINVAL. Any other iter_kind returns -EINVAL. On every -EINVAL return the iterator has been reset (it->p is NULL) and its desc is not set. On success it sets it->vlen to btf_vlen(t) when the descriptor has per-member entries, sets it->p = t and returns 0.
note: tools/lib/bpf/btf_iter.c:16-143. Reviewer right: the old text excluded unsupported iter_kind as a precondition yet also described -EINVAL for it; the code returns -EINVAL for both an unsupported iter_kind (134-135) and an unsupported BTF kind. Contract left empty.

name: libbpf_reallocarray
prose: Static inline wrapper: ptr is the block to resize, nmemb and size give the new element count and size. Returns NULL without calling realloc if nmemb * size overflows size_t. When the compiler has __builtin_mul_overflow the test is just that overflow check (so a zero product, for example size 0, is passed on); otherwise the fallback test also returns NULL when size is 0 or nmemb is above ULONG_MAX / size. In all other cases it returns realloc(ptr, nmemb * size): with the builtin and a zero product that is realloc(ptr, 0), whose result and effect on ptr are those of the C library; with the fallback a zero size returns NULL and leaves ptr untouched. On a NULL return from the overflow checks ptr is not freed.
note: libbpf_internal.h:206-219. Reviewer right: the fallback path (214-215) returns NULL for size == 0, while the builtin path reaches realloc(ptr, 0). Which path is used depends on __has_builtin(__builtin_mul_overflow).

name: __sw_hweight64
prose: Population count of a 64-bit word w, returned as unsigned long (0 to 64). With 32-bit longs it returns __sw_hweight32 of the high 32 bits plus __sw_hweight32 of the low 32 bits. With 64-bit longs and CONFIG_ARCH_HAS_FAST_MULTIPLIER it does the usual bit-parallel reduction (pairs, nibbles, bytes) and returns (w * 0x0101010101010101) >> 56; without the fast multiplier it adds the bytes by shifting (res + (res >> 8), >> 16, >> 32) and returns that masked with 0xff. Both give the number of set bits of w. It reads no other state and has no side effects.
note: tools/lib/hweight.c:43-63. Reviewer (the old contract is false for w = 65536 with result 65536) right: the result is the bit count, 1 for w = 65536. Contract left empty.

name: read_perf_counter
prose: x86 inline-assembly helper: counter is the performance-counter index. It executes the rdpmc instruction with ecx = counter, reading the low and high halves into eax and edx, and returns low | (high << 32). It has no checks: on a CPU or privilege setting where user-mode rdpmc is not allowed, or for a counter index that is not valid, the instruction faults (the function traps). No other state is read or written.
note: tools/lib/perf/mmap.c:295-302 (the x86 variant; other architectures define their own read_perf_counter, lines 364, 465, 476). Reviewer right that it can trap for inputs a plain integer contract would accept. Contract left empty.

name: perf_mmap__read_self
prose: Precondition: map is a perf mmap with map->base pointing to a perf_event_mmap_page (or NULL) and count receives the result. Returns -1 if the page is NULL or cap_user_rdpmc is not set, else 0 on success and -1 if, inside the retry loop, cap_user_rdpmc is not set or the counter index is 0. It loops with the page's sequence lock: reads seq, copies time_enabled and time_running into count->ena and count->run, and, when cap_user_time is set and ena differs from run, reads the timestamp (read_timestamp) and the time_mult, time_shift, time_offset and, if cap_user_time_short, time_cycles and time_mask. It reads index and offset; if cap_user_rdpmc and idx are nonzero it reads the hardware counter idx - 1 with read_perf_counter, truncates it to pmc_width bits (shifting left then right by 64 - width) and adds it to the offset; otherwise it returns -1 at once (count->ena and run were already written). It repeats while pc->lock differs from seq. After the loop, if ena differs from run it adjusts the cycle count for the short-time capability, computes delta = time_offset + mul_u64_u32_shr(cyc, time_mult, time_shift) (these time values stay 0 when cap_user_time was not set) and adds delta to count->ena, and also to count->run when idx is nonzero. It stores the counter in count->val and returns 0.
note: Listed as perf_counter_read_seqlock_fragment (dropped); the slice (mmap.c:508-539) is the tail of perf_mmap__read_self (480-539), a real function, so fixed under its real name. read_perf_counter and read_timestamp are architecture-specific helpers defined above it.

name: wait_or_whine
prose: Precondition: cmd is a child_process with pid, finished and finish_result; block selects a blocking wait. It starts from the cached finished flag and finish_result. While not finished it calls waitpid(cmd->pid, &status, block ? 0 : WNOHANG): a nonblocking call returning 0 leaves the loop with finished still false (cmd is not modified in that case); EINTR retries; any other outcome sets finished. The result is then: waitpid error: prints a message and -ERR_RUN_COMMAND_WAITPID; a pid other than cmd->pid: -ERR_RUN_COMMAND_WAITPID_WRONG_PID; terminated by a signal: -ERR_RUN_COMMAND_WAITPID_SIGNAL; not exited: -ERR_RUN_COMMAND_WAITPID_NOEXIT; exit status 127: -ERR_RUN_COMMAND_EXEC; status 0: 0; any other status: minus the exit code. After the loop, whenever finished is true (including when cmd->finished was already set on entry), it writes cmd->finished = 1 and cmd->finish_result = result; it returns result (the cached finish_result when it was already finished).
note: tools/lib/subcmd/run-command.c:170-218. Reviewer right: line 213-216 write cmd->finished and cmd->finish_result even when finished was already set (with the same values), so 'without touching cmd' was wrong.

name: add_list
prose: Precondition: buf holds one page-owner record of len bytes, ext_buf the extra buffer used by get_allocator; the global list has max_size entries. Returns false with an error message if list_size equals max_size, returns true without adding anything if is_need(buf) is false (filtering). Otherwise it fills list[list_size] with pid, tgid and comm from the record, mallocs a copy of the text (len + 1 bytes; on failure it prints 'Out of memory' and returns false after the pid, tgid and comm fields were already stored and comm is not freed), copies it, and, unless the first sort key is compare_ts, removes the timestamp pattern from the copy (updating len); it NUL-terminates the copy, stores len, sets num to 1, stores page_num, sets stacktrace to the text after the first newline (or to "" when there is none), stores ts_nsec and allocator, increments list_size and, every 1000 entries, prints a progress line and flushes stdout. It then returns true. get_comm always returns the allocated string (its NULL branch is unreachable because errno is cleared right before the test), so comm is non-NULL unless the malloc inside get_comm failed (not checked there).
note: slice cut the head; real function page_owner_sort.c:474-510 with get_comm (373-389) and is_need (455-472) read. Reviewer right: get_comm sets errno = 0 (380) immediately before testing it (381), so its NULL return is unreachable.

name: main
prose: Entry point of page_owner_sort: argv holds options, an input file and an output file. Options -a, -d, -m, -p, -s, -t, -P, -n set compare flags (or debug); --pid, --tgid and --name set filters (an unparsable pid or tgid list exits with status 1), --cull and --sort parse their arguments (failure exits with 1); any other option prints usage and exit(1). If fewer than two positional arguments remain it prints usage and exit(1). It selects a single comparison function from the compare flag (ALLOC gives compare_ts ascending, PAGE_NUM page number descending, PID, STACK, TGID and COMM ascending, none or NUM compare_num descending); any other combination of flags prints usage and exit(1). It opens the input and output files (failure: usage, perror, exit(1)), then compiles five regexes (order, pid, tgid, comm, timestamp) with check_regcomp; a failure at one goes to the label for that pattern, which regfree's that pattern and all patterns compiled before it (not the later ones), and the function returns 0. It sizes the list as the file size / 100, mallocs the list and two buffers (failure prints 'Out of memory' and goes to out_free), reads records with read_block and adds them with add_list (a false result goes to out_free), sorts, merges equal entries by summing num and page_num, sorts again and prints each entry either in full or with the culled fields. out_free frees the buffers and list, then the regexes are freed, and the function returns 0; every path that reaches the end, including the failures handled by goto, returns 0, while the explicit exit(1) calls leave earlier. The input and output FILE objects are not closed.
note: slice cut the head; real function page_owner_sort.c:665-891. Reviewer right: the out_* labels free only the pattern that failed and those compiled before it (lines 796-805, 879-888), not all five.

name: slab_debug
prose: Precondition: s is a slabinfo entry; the globals sanity, redzone, poison, tracking, tracing and slabs describe the requested flags and the number of selected slabs. Returns nothing. It returns at once for the entry named "*". Then, for each flag, it applies the change only when the requested state differs from the slab's current state: sanity_checks, red_zone, poison and store_user (tracking) can be switched on or off with set_obj only when slab_empty(s) is true (the sanity checks are switched on without that condition), otherwise it prints 'not empty cannot ...' to stderr and leaves the setting alone. Tracing is different: enabling trace (tracing set and s->trace clear) is done with set_obj only when the global slabs equals 1, otherwise it prints 'can only enable trace for one slab at a time'; slab_empty is not consulted for trace; disabling trace (tracing clear and s->trace set) is done unconditionally. No value is returned.
note: tools/mm/slabinfo.c:744-802. Reviewer right: enabling trace depends on slabs == 1 only (794-798), not on slab_empty(s); also enabling sanity checks (749-751) has no emptiness condition.

name: arch_dest_reloc_offset
prose: Pure helper for the loongarch objtool backend: it returns its int argument addend converted to unsigned long (return addend). A negative addend is therefore sign-extended and becomes a very large unsigned value (addend -1 gives ULONG_MAX); a non-negative addend is returned unchanged. No other state is read or written.
note: tools/objtool/arch/loongarch/decode.c:20-23. Reviewer (random testing: the old contract result == addend is false for a negative addend) right: the result is the unsigned conversion of addend.

name: check
prose: Entry point of objtool's check pass: file is the objtool_file for one object. Returns 0 only when ret is 0 and no warnings were counted; otherwise it returns ret, which is set to 1 when the werror option is on and warnings were counted (a nonzero ret already set by an earlier step is kept). It initialises the CFI states, allocates the CFI hash (ret = -1 on failure, then goes to out), adds the initial states, runs decode_sections (nonzero result goes to out) and goes to out if there are no instructions. Then, depending on options: it adds the warning counts of validate_retpoline, validate_functions / validate_unwind_hints / validate_reachable_instructions (the last only if the first two reported none) or validate_noinstr_sections, validate_unrets, validate_ibt and validate_sls. It then creates the output sections, each step jumping to out with its nonzero result: static_call, retpoline sites, CFI, return sites (and direct calls with hack_skylake), mcount locations, prefix symbols and the IBT endbr seal sections; adds the warning count of check_abs_references with noabs; calls orc_create (error goes to out) when orc is set and there are instructions; frees the instructions and prints statistics if requested. At out it returns 0 if there was neither an error nor a warning; with werror and warnings it forces ret to 1; with verbose it prints the warning-upgrade message, the arguments and the functions with warnings; and returns ret. Warnings alone, without the werror option, do not change ret, so the function returns 0 in that case.
note: Listed as an unnamed driver body (dropped); the slice (check.c:4821-4908) is the tail of check (4770-4908), a real function, so fixed. Old prose said it returned the first failing pass's code or 1 for werror; warnings without werror still return ret (0). The validate_* and create_* helpers were not read.

name: arm_spe_snapshot_resolve_auxtrace_defaults
prose: Precondition: opts is the perf record_opts with auxtrace_snapshot_size, auxtrace_mmap_pages (0 means not given) and mmap_pages (UINT_MAX means not given); privileged says whether the user is privileged; page_size is a global. Returns nothing. If neither the snapshot size nor the auxtrace mmap pages is given: privileged users get auxtrace_mmap_pages = MiB(4) / page_size; unprivileged users get KiB(128) / page_size and, if mmap_pages is UINT_MAX, mmap_pages = KiB(256) / page_size. Otherwise, if auxtrace_mmap_pages is 0 for an unprivileged user and mmap_pages is UINT_MAX, mmap_pages is set to KiB(256) / page_size. Then, if no snapshot size is given it is set to auxtrace_mmap_pages * page_size. Finally, if auxtrace_mmap_pages is still 0 it is set to the snapshot size rounded up to a whole number of pages and then up to a power of two, in pages. Values already given are left unchanged.
note: arm-spe.c:188-235 (slice cut the head). Reviewer right: the 'mmap_pages unspecified' sentinel is UINT_MAX (lines 211 and 214), not 0; a zero auxtrace_mmap_pages is what means unspecified for that field.

name: arch_skip_callchain_idx
prose: Precondition: thread is the sampled thread and chain a perf ip_callchain whose slot 1 is the program counter and slot 2 the link register. Returns the index of the callchain slot to ignore (2 or 3) or -1 (skip_slot starts as the u64 value -1 and is returned through an int). It returns -1 at once if chain is NULL or chain->nr is below 3. Otherwise it initialises an addr_location, resolves ips[1] with thread__find_symbol for user mode, takes the dso of the found map (a missing map or dso logs a debug message, exits the addr_location and returns -1), calls check_return_addr(dso, map start, ip) and logs the result (the log line dereferences al.sym->name, so al.sym is assumed non-NULL when debug output is built). A result of 0 (return address on the stack, ignore the LR value) gives 2 and a result of 2 (new frame allocated but the return address still in LR) gives 3; any other result leaves -1. It then exits the addr_location and returns the slot.
note: Listed as an unnamed excerpt; the slice (skip-callchain-idx.c:253-287) is the tail of arch_skip_callchain_idx (242-287), a real function, so fixed. check_return_addr (152-217) read: it returns -1 on DWARF failures else check_return_reg's value.

name: update_insn_state_x86
prose: Precondition: state is the tracked register and stack type state, dloc the data-location info, cu_die the DWARF compile unit, dl the disassembled instruction. Returns nothing; it updates state in place and returns early in many cases. It first gets the instruction's operand locations with annotate_get_insn_location and returns if that fails. For a call: it returns with no change if the target symbol is unknown or is __fentry__; otherwise it marks every caller-saved register not ok, and if the callee's return type is found in DWARF it sets the return register to that type (kind TSR_KIND_TYPE, ok true), then returns. For an instruction whose name starts with "add": it returns unless the destination register is tracked; it takes an immediate, a constant register value, or a PC-relative address of a global (the variable "this_cpu_off" turns a constant register into TSR_KIND_PERCPU_BASE), returns for other forms, returns unless the register kind is PERCPU_BASE, and if a global variable type is found at the immediate with offset 0 it makes the register a TSR_KIND_PERCPU_POINTER of that type. Instructions not named "mov*" return. For a mov: with fb_cfa it derives the frame base register from the CFA at the instruction. Register to register (no memory operand): the destination is cleared of copied_from; a gs-relative immediate in kernel code is the stack canary (kind TSR_KIND_CANARY, offset 40) or a per-cpu variable whose member type is looked up (the destination is not ok if not found); an immediate becomes TSR_KIND_CONST; otherwise the source register's type, kind and value are copied if the source is tracked and ok, else the destination is marked not ok. Memory to register: a source based on the frame or stack register is looked up in the tracked stack slots (type copied, member type for compound slots, else not ok); a tracked typed pointer register is dereferenced with die_deref_ptr_type; a PC-relative source is looked up as a global variable and member; a PERCPU_BASE source register (optionally plus a constant second register) is looked up as a per-cpu variable; a PERCPU_POINTER source gets its member type; a two-register source retries with the second register; otherwise, for a negative source offset naming the variable __per_cpu_offset the destination becomes kind TSR_KIND_PERCPU_BASE with ok true (this is the mov path that sets PERCPU_BASE), else the destination is marked not ok. Register to memory: if the source register is tracked and ok and the destination is a stack or frame slot it records or updates the stack slot state with the register's kind and type.
note: slice cut the head; real function instructions.c:212-607 (x86 variant of the function under CONFIG_... guards up to line 608); read with debug-print lines filtered out, so exact debug text and a few intermediate lines (439-445, 477-482, 553-556, 576-583) were skimmed rather than read in full. Reviewer right: the mov memory-to-register path can set TSR_KIND_PERCPU_BASE with ok true for __per_cpu_offset (546-551), which the old prose omitted.

name: main
prose: Test-data program for the x86 instruction decoder (insn-x86-dat-src.c): main takes no arguments and consists of a long list of asm volatile statements (4009 in the file, 27 to 3136 under #ifdef __x86_64__ and 3137 to 5354 for the 32-bit variant, with some shared ones before and after) that exist so their encodings appear in the compiled output for the decoder tests; the program is not meant to be run. The body starts with an asm volatile("rdtsc") start marker comment-tagged for the awk script and ends with another rdtsc marker followed by its only return, return 0. The instructions are straight-line, with no branches, loops, calls or gotos, so if executed it would run them in order (many require CPU features the host may not have, and executing them could fault) and return 0. It does not read or write program data of its own.
note: slice cut the head; real function insn-x86-dat-src.c:18-5479; structure checked with grep (a single return at line 5478, no goto), the instruction list was not read in full. Reviewer right that the old contract (result == 0) omitted the execution-order and side-effect statements; contract left empty because of the inline assembly.

name: bench_futex_requeue
prose: Entry point of the perf futex-requeue benchmark: argc and argv are the command line. It parses options; leftover non-option arguments go to err, which prints usage and calls exit(EXIT_FAILURE) (so that path does not return). Otherwise it gets the online cpu map (err(EXIT_FAILURE) if that fails), installs a SIGINT handler, optionally mlockall (err(EXIT_FAILURE) on failure), defaults nthreads to the number of online CPUs, callocs the worker array (err(EXIT_FAILURE) on failure), sets the private futex flag when not shared, caps nrequeue to nthreads (or sets it to nthreads for broadcast), prints a run summary and initialises stats and locks. It then repeats bench_repeat times (stopping when interrupted): it starts the worker threads blocked on futex1, waits until all are started, sleeps 100 ms, and requeues in a loop with futex_cmp_requeue (or the PI variant, counting one wakeup each time) until nthreads have been requeued, an error result calling err(EXIT_FAILURE, ...) (not usage); it records the elapsed time, prints it unless silent, wakes the requeued threads on futex2 in the non-PI case (a count mismatch only warns) and joins every worker with pthread_join (a nonzero result calls err(EXIT_FAILURE)). After the runs it destroys the condition variables and mutex, prints the summary, frees the worker array, releases the cpu map and returns ret, which is 0 unless a pthread_join result was nonzero (which would already have exited).
note: slice cut the head; real function futex-requeue.c:169-319. Reviewer right: fatal failures (requeue, pthread_join, allocation, cpu map) call err(EXIT_FAILURE, ...) and exit directly; only leftover arguments print usage (176-178, 316-318).

name: bench_synthesize
prose: Entry point of the perf synthesize benchmark (the function listed as main): argc and argv are the command line. It parses options with parse_options; if any non-option argument remains it prints usage and calls exit(EXIT_FAILURE) (it does not return in that case). If neither the single-threaded nor the multi-threaded run is requested it enables the single-threaded run. It runs run_single_threaded() if requested, and then run_multi_threaded() only if the first run (if any) returned 0 and the multi-threaded run is requested. It returns the last err value: 0 or the nonzero result of the first failing run.
note: Listed as main; the real function is bench_synthesize, synthesize.c:249-273 (the file has no main). Mechanical name rejection only; written from the code.

name: lockf
prose: Local replacement for lockf (builtin-daemon.c:1123-1129, compiled only when F_TLOCK is not defined by the system headers, together with a fallback #define F_TLOCK 2): fd is an open file descriptor, cmd and len are the lockf command and length. It returns -1 immediately, without touching fd, unless cmd is F_TLOCK and len is 0. Otherwise it returns flock(fd, LOCK_EX | LOCK_NB): 0 when the exclusive non-blocking lock was taken, or -1 with errno set (for example EWOULDBLOCK when it is already locked, EBADF for a bad descriptor). The lock belongs to the open file description and stays until the descriptor is closed or unlocked. No other state is changed.
note: Reviewer right (the old contract omitted the fd precondition and the lock semantics). Contract left empty because the function depends on a system call.

name: cmd_daemon
prose: Entry point of 'perf daemon': argc and argv are the sub-command line. Returns an int: 0 or the sub-command's result, -1 for an unknown command, or -ENOMEM. ret starts as -1. It sets __daemon.perf = alloc_perf_exe_path(); if that returns NULL (the field is then NULL) it returns -ENOMEM at once. Otherwise it sets the output to stdout and parses the global options (verbose, config, base, field-separator) stopping at the first non-option. If a sub-command remains: "start", "signal", "stop" and "ping" run __cmd_start, __cmd_signal, __cmd_stop and __cmd_ping and ret is their result; any other word prints 'failed: unknown command' and leaves ret at its initial -1. With no sub-command it calls setup_config(&__daemon); a nonzero result prints 'failed: config not found' and is the return value; otherwise ret is the result of send_cmd_list. Before returning it frees __daemon.perf with zfree (which also sets it to NULL).
note: slice cut the head; real function builtin-daemon.c:1500-1543. Reviewer MIXED: the unknown-command path does return -1 (ret is initialised to -1 at 1512 and not changed at 1533), so 'does not return -1' is wrong; it is right that __daemon.perf is NULL when the allocation fails (the -ENOMEM path).

name: cmd_help
prose: Entry point of 'perf help': argc and argv are the sub-command line. Returns an int: 0 for the listing cases, a nonzero result of perf_config, or the result of the page viewer. It loads the command list, calls perf_config(perf_help_config, &help_format) and returns its result at once if nonzero. It parses options (-a/--all, -m/--man, -w/--web, -i/--info); the parsed argc is not used afterwards, the function tests argv[0]. With --all it prints the usage string, the list of commands and the more-info string and returns 0. With no command argument (argv[0] is NULL) it prints usage, the common command list and the more-info string and returns 0. Otherwise it selects by help_format: HELP_FORMAT_MAN returns show_man_page(argv[0]), which tries the configured viewers, then the PERF_MAN_VIEWER fallback and "man" (each exec only returns on failure) and then logs and returns -1; HELP_FORMAT_INFO returns show_info_page(argv[0]); HELP_FORMAT_WEB returns show_html_page(argv[0]), which returns -1 if get_html_page_path fails (and 0 after open_html, which normally does not return because it execs a browser); HELP_FORMAT_NONE and any other value return -1.
note: slice cut the head; real function builtin-help.c:430-499. Reviewer right: the web path can return -1 from show_html_page (418-423), which the old prose omitted. show_info_page and open_html were not read.

name: mark_dso_hit
prose: Precondition: inject, tool, sample, machine, mmap_evsel, map describe the injection context; sample_in_dso says whether the sample's cpumode already matches the map. Always returns 0 (the only two returns are 0). It returns at once when map is NULL. If sample_in_dso is false it recomputes the cpu mode: it keeps only the hypervisor bit of the sample's mode and adds the guest kernel or guest user bit when the sample was a guest sample, or the kernel or user bit otherwise, according to whether the map is a kernel map. It takes the map's dso. With build_id_style BID_RWS__INJECT_HEADER_LAZY, if the dso exists and is not yet marked hit, it marks it hit and injects a build id event for it (tool__inject_build_id with the long name and map flags). With BID_RWS__MMAP2_BUILDID_LAZY, only if map__hit(map) is false it marks the map hit and synthesises an mmap2-with-build-id event (using the dso's build id and long name, or an empty id and name when there is no dso) and repipes it. With any other build_id_style nothing is injected. The guard on map__hit applies to the mmap2 case and the dso hit flag applies to the header case, so each map or dso is processed at most once for the respective style.
note: slice cut the head; real function builtin-inject.c:926-985. Reviewer right: the mmap2 lazy branch only acts when !map__hit(map) (964), which the old prose omitted.

name: cmd_kmem
prose: Entry point of 'perf kmem': argc and argv are the sub-command line. Returns an int. It first calls perf_config(kmem_config, NULL) and returns its nonzero result. It parses options (input, verbose, caller, alloc, sort, line, raw-ip, force, slab, page, live, time) stopping at the first non-option; if no sub-command remains it calls usage_with_options (which exits). If neither slab nor page analysis was selected it picks the default one. If argv[0] is a prefix of "record" of more than two characters it initialises symbols and returns __cmd_record(argc, argv). Otherwise it opens a perf session on the input (a failure returns the PTR_ERR value), sets ret to -1 and checks for the needed tracepoint events: for slab analysis the kmem:kmalloc event, for page analysis the kmem:mm_page_alloc event with its format (it records the page size and enables callchains); a missing event prints 'No ... allocation events found' and goes to out_delete returning -1. It initialises symbols and parses the time range (an invalid string gives -EINVAL, via out_delete). Only now is the sub-command checked: for "stat" it sets the locale, sets up the cpunode map (failure goes to out_delete returning -1), sets up default sort keys and, for page analysis, the page input sort keys, and ret = __cmd_kmem(session); for any other sub-command it calls usage_with_options, which exits. So the early returns (event not found, bad time string) happen before an unknown sub-command reaches the usage call. out_delete deletes the session, frees the usage string and returns ret.
note: slice cut the head; real function builtin-kmem.c:1931-2066. Reviewer right: for an unknown sub-command usage is called only after the session, event checks and time parsing, each of which can return -1 or -EINVAL first (2002-2033, 2057-2058).
